extracted.intended_audience: school pupils or students studying the North Carolina Constitution and state history (civics/classroom readers)
extracted.subtask_description: A Q&A study guide listing what students should know about the North Carolina Constitution: the judiciary, taxation, suffrage, municipal and corporate powers, education, homesteads, punishments and charitable institutions, militia, amendment procedures, and miscellaneous constitutional provisions. Each Article's key points and questions are enumerated for memorization and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article IV — Judiciary: appointments, jurisdiction, terms, and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Know who appoints/ elects judicial officers (Justices of the Supreme Court, Superior Court Judges, Clerks), their terms of office, when elections occur, who prescribes salaries/fees, and how judicial independence is secured; understand what laws are in force (including 'Common Law' and where to find it), who can alter laws, the effect of a Judge's findings on facts, treatment of pending actions when the Constitution took effect, provisions for creating other courts and choosing officers, grounds/notice/vote required for removal of judges and clerks, appeal rights for clerks and inferior courts, and whether certain sections are obsolete. (Questions referenced: Sections 13–33 and related parts of Article IV as cited throughout the question list.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes many specific questions: appointment and term of Supreme Court Clerk (Secs. 15–16), appointment/election/terms of Superior Court judges and clerks (Secs. 16–22, 29–30), jurisdiction of Justices of the Peace (Sec. 27), appeals, jury provisions, records and duties of Justices (Sec. 27), filling vacancies (Secs. 24–29), removal procedures (Sec. 31), and notes on 'Common Law' sources (reports, writings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article V — Revenues and Taxation: tax types, limits, and restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to define capitation (poll) tax, know whether the General Assembly is required to levy it and on whom, the maximum capitation and property tax rates (e.g., sixty-six and two-thirds cents per $100 valuation), the object of 'equation of taxes', who may exempt from capitation tax and for what reason, purposes to which capitation tax must be applied, limits on amounts applied to support the poor, how property must be taxed, what the General Assembly may tax without compulsion, tax treatment of a farmer's land income, provisions regarding contracting new debts and special taxes (including when special taxes are required or not depending on bond par value), rules before the Assembly can give the State's credit or take stock in corporations, what property the Assembly cannot tax or may exempt (unlimited/limited exemptions and limits), how county taxes are levied and limits of county taxation for general purposes, procedures when counties seek to exceed limits for special purposes, requirements for levying 'Revenue Acts', and whether tax money raised for one purpose may be used for another. (Questions reference Article V, Sections 1–7 and related.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes specifics on maximum rates (capitation and property), 'equation of taxes' rationale, voting or majority requirements for debt/credit questions, Supreme Court note on State taking stock (cannot), and cross-references to county taxation limits (Article V Sec. 6) and Revenue Acts (Sec. 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article VI — Suffrage and Eligibility to Office: voter qualifications and office-holding
rubrics_metrics.description: Master qualifications of an elector (voter), exceptions to voter qualifications, whether mere commission of an infamous crime disqualifies, which authority determines restoration of citizenship rights, prerequisites to voting (registration steps and required oath), what authority provides registration rules, how the people and members of the General Assembly vote in officer elections (and cross-reference to Article II Sec. 9), general qualifications for holding office, required oaths for officers, persons disqualified from office, and whether mere disbelief in God disqualifies unless expressed ('deny' interpreted as assertion of disbelief). (Questions reference Article VI, Sections 1–4 and Article I Sec. 26.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes both voter registration process (oaths, rules) and distinctions between private belief and expressed denial regarding religious qualification for office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article VII — Municipal Corporations: county and township officers, powers, and statutory changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Know what county officers are elected and how often elections occur; the constitutional duties of County Commissioners; how those duties were modified by the Acts of 1876–'77 (chapter 141) — e.g., Commissioners' restricted powers (levy taxes, purchase land, borrow money, etc.) and their new supervisory role over townships; who is Clerk of Commissioners; formation and naming of districts and their powers; composition and appointment/terms of Township Boards/Trustees and Justices of the Peace under the 1876–'77 act; other township officers; changes to section 6 under later acts (e.g., 1881 chapter 117 concerning listing and tax lists); what is necessary for counties/municipal corporations to contract debts, pledge credit, or levy taxes beyond necessary expenses (majority sufficiency question); rules for drawing funds from county treasuries; taxation rules and required/allowed exemptions; whether particular sections (10,11) are obsolete; effect of adoption of Article on prior charters; forbidden county debts; what provisions the General Assembly can change or abrogate; and special notes about election of County Superintendents of Public Instruction (Act of 1881, chapter 200).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contains specific statutory cross-references to Acts of 1876–'77 and 1881 and details about the transfer of powers between Commissioners and Justices of the Peace; students should note procedural and statutory amendments called out in the study questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article VIII — Corporations other than municipal: formation, charters, liabilities, and legislative restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the ways corporations may be formed (general law or special act), cases where special act creation is appropriate, whether charters granted under this section may be amended or repealed, how debts of corporations shall be secured, who prescribes rules for securing corporate dues, the meaning of 'corporation' as used in the Article, whether corporations can sue and be sued like natural persons, which authority organizes cities/towns/incorporated villages, and what powers the General Assembly should restrict and the purposes of those restrictions. (Questions reference Article VIII, Sections 1–4.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the balance between corporate powers, legislative oversight, and the treatment of corporations as legal persons; includes procedural and policy considerations for limiting municipal powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article IX — Education: duties of Assembly, school structure, funds, and Board of Education powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to explain why schools should be encouraged, the duty of the General Assembly regarding public schools and how they must provide them, school ages and required duration, tuition charge rules, permissibility of 'mixed schools' and equality between races, county division for school purposes, maintenance duration and penalties for Commissioners' failure, what funds are set aside for support and whether they can be used for other purposes, which officer manages these funds, county funds for schools and how the Superintendent of Public Instruction learns about them, election and powers of University Trustees and their legislative/management duties, the Assembly's duty toward university education, treatment of escheats and unclaimed dividends, composition and officers of the State Board of Education, succession to previous bodies, legislative power vested in the Board and whether such legislation is final, meeting times and quorum, contingent expense provision, required University departments, and whether the General Assembly can enact compulsory education (over what ages and for what length of time). (Questions reference Article IX, Sections 1–15 and related.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes explicit questions on segregation/equality in schools, fund separations, administrative structure (Board, Trustees, Superintendent), and the possibility/limits of compulsory education (Sec. 15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article X — Homesteads and Exemptions: what property is exempt and family rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Know how much personal property is exempt from execution and who chooses it, whether the exemption is only from execution, what land is exempt and its value, who selects the homestead and whether a city lot can be set apart, homestead liability for taxes and other debts, duration of homestead exemption after owner's death, whether a homestead is exempt from mechanic's/laborer's liens for work done, widow's rights and duration in case of owner dying with widow but no children, privileges of the widow and who is entitled, property of a woman on marriage and property acquired after marriage (ownership between husband and wife), whether such property can pay husband's debts, whether she can will it, whether husband's assent is necessary for validity of her will or for sale/gift of her separate property, whether husband's assent may be by word of mouth, ability to insure life for benefit of wife/children and effect on creditors, disposition of insurance money at death, whether an unmarried owner can sell the homestead and requirements for validity of deed. (Questions reference Article X, Sections 1–8.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers both procedural/formal requirements (validity of deeds, assent rules) and substantive family-property protections (homestead exemptions, widow's privileges, married woman's property rights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article XI — Punishments, Penal Institutions, and Public Charities: lawful punishments, institutions, and care duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify what punishments are lawful in North Carolina, whether convicts can labor on public works or be hired/farmed out and limits on farming out, which convicts cannot be farmed out, who prescribes rules on farming out and whether hirers can punish convicts freely, what punishments may be imposed by proper officers, under whose supervision convicts are, whether the General Assembly can abolish capital punishment and for which offenses death can be inflicted, objectives of punishment, duties of the General Assembly regarding penitentiaries, purposes for houses of correction and houses of refuge, required arrangements for structure and superintendence of penal institutions, provisions regarding male and female prisoners, the state's duty toward pauper, indigent, orphans (first duties of a civilized State), required actions by the General Assembly and duties of the Board overseeing such institutions, obligations toward destitute orphans and idiots (including educational possibilities), other classes to be provided for at State expense, changes to language of sections by amendment (e.g., substitution of 'may' for 'must'), and whether penal and charitable institutions should be made self-supporting. (Questions reference Article XI, Sections 1–11 and related amendments.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes institutional structure (penitentiary, houses of correction/refuge), supervision and statutory rules for convict labor, capital punishment policy, and the state's charitable duties and administrative responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article XII — Militia: liability, exemptions, and Assembly duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Know who is liable to militia duty and who is exempt, the duties of the General Assembly regarding the militia, who is Commander-in-Chief of the militia and under what authority (cross-reference to Article III), for what purposes the militia may be called out, what authority can make exemptions from militia duty, and any other duties the General Assembly has regarding militia organization and regulation. (Questions reference Article XII, Sections 1–4 and connections to Article III Sections 7–8.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes both individual liability/exemption questions and legislative/ executive powers over calling out and regulating the militia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article XIII — Amendments: conventions versus legislative amendment procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand how a convention of the people must be called (who, manner, and authority directing submission and day of meeting), the number of votes necessary in the Senate and House to call such conventions (e.g., two-thirds thresholds), what a convention may do (amend or make a new Constitution), the concept of a 'restricted convention' and whether the General Assembly can bind members' actions, whether the Constitution can be altered without calling a Convention, by what vote proposed changes must pass the General Assembly (three-fifths), whether that means three-fifths of all members of each House and the smallest numeric majorities required, what must be done with a proposed amendment after legislative passage, whether it requires a majority of all qualified voters to pass, and comparative questions about two-thirds versus three-fifths thresholds. (Questions reference Article XIII, Sections 1–2.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights procedural thresholds (two-thirds vs three-fifths), submission and voter-majority requirements, and the option/limits of restricted conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article XIV — Miscellaneous provisions: pending indictments, dueling, offices, marriages, and other rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Know rules for pending indictments at adoption of the Constitution, rules regarding dueling and disqualification of challenger/challenged/carriers when fights do or do not occur, whether citizens fighting in another State violate NC law (answer: not per se but agreeing to go out of State to fight is an offense), what is necessary to draw money from the State Treasury and required accounting of receipts/expenditures, protections to mechanics and laborers (cross-reference to Article X Sec. 4), general provisions on terms of office, seat of government, rules regarding holding double office and exceptions, prohibited marriages and the racial proportion that triggers the prohibition (one-eighth negro blood/octoroon), and other miscellaneous constitutional provisions as listed. (Questions reference Article XIV, Sections 1–8 and cross-references.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contains practical governance and social rule questions (treasury accounting, marriage prohibitions, dual-office rules), plus specific racial threshold noted (octoroon = one-eighth) for marriage prohibition.
